The New York City subway has a reputation for being dangerous. For the Exploratory Data
Analysis course at GW (Prof. John Helveston, fall 2025), four of us tested that
reputation against six public datasets from the MTA, the NYPD, and NYC Open Data, all
analyzed in R.

The short answer was that riding the subway is safer than the reputation suggests.
Once crime is measured per rider rather than in raw counts, the risk on any one trip is
low, and service breakdowns turned out to have only a weak link to crime.

### What I did

- Normalized MTA crime by ridership. Raw felony counts fell in 2020, but ridership
  fell much faster, so the per-rider rate briefly spiked. Measuring crime per million
  riders separates that effect from any real change in safety.
- Tested whether a breakdown-heavy month is also a high-crime month. I totaled the
  MTA's signal, track, and subway-car incidents by month, joined them to monthly felony
  counts on the subway, and fit a linear trend. The correlation was weak (r = 0.23).
- Built both charts below in ggplot2, using the tidyverse for the cleaning and joins.
- With the team, compared subway crime with citywide crime and traffic crashes, and
  mapped shootings within 40 meters of each station in Leaflet.

### My charts

![Major felonies per million MTA riders, by month.](/images/projects/nyc-subway-crime-per-million.png){fig-alt="Line chart of total major felonies per million MTA riders by month, 2019 to 2025. The rate sits around 3 to 4 before 2020, spikes to about 33 in spring 2020 as ridership collapses, then fluctuates mostly between 5 and 20, with occasional spikes up to about 30."}

The spike in spring 2020 comes from ridership falling much faster than felonies did.
Since then the rate has been noisier and higher than before the pandemic, mostly between
5 and 20 felonies per million riders, which is still a small risk on any one trip.

![Monthly operational incidents against monthly felonies on the subway. Each point is one month.](/images/projects/nyc-subway-incidents-vs-crime.png){fig-alt="Scatterplot of monthly operational incidents (0 to about 60) against monthly felony counts on the subway (about 85 to 265), one point per month, with a shallow upward linear trend line labeled r = 0.23. The points are widely scattered around the line."}

The trend slopes up, but months with similar incident totals vary widely in crime.
Breakdowns on their own do not explain much of the subway's crime.
